lead: A blood gas analyser measures the three variables that set the acid–base state of arterial blood: pH, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO₂) and the partial pressure of oxygen (pO₂). Three electrodes sit in one chamber held at 37 °C. A glass pH electrode, a Severinghaus pCO₂ electrode and a Clark pO₂ electrode produce electrical signals, and the analyser calculates bicarbonate and base excess from them. It is used in emergency rooms, intensive care and operation theatres, where a patient in ketoacidosis or on a ventilator needs the result within minutes.
prereq: You need electrode theory and the Nernst equation from Unit 1, and the readout and calibration ideas are close to those in 3.1.

blocks.text: pH tells how acidic a solution is. It is defined as pH = −log₁₀ a(H⁺), where a(H⁺) is the hydrogen ion activity in mol/L. In dilute blood, activity is close to concentration, so pH ≈ −log₁₀[H⁺]. Arterial blood normally lies between 7.35 and 7.45; below 7.35 is acidaemia and above 7.45 is alkalaemia.

blocks.where: a(H⁺) is the hydrogen ion activity in mol/L; [H⁺] is the hydrogen ion concentration in mol/L.

blocks.text: The measurement is potentiometric. The measuring electrode is a glass bulb with a thin hydrated layer. H⁺ ions exchange at the glass surface and create a potential that depends on pH. The reference electrode is Ag/AgCl in fixed KCl; it gives a constant potential. The analyser measures the voltage between the two electrodes. The glass electrode has very high resistance, so the amplifier must have high input impedance; otherwise the reading loads the cell and falls.

blocks.where: E is the electrode potential in volts; E⁰ is the standard potential; R is 8.314 J/(mol·K); T is absolute temperature in K; n is the number of electrons per ion (n = 1 for H⁺); F is 96485 C/mol; a is activity.

blocks.text: For H⁺, the practical form is E = E⁰ − (2.303RT/F) pH. At 37 °C the slope 2.303RT/F is about 61.5 mV per pH unit. One pH unit changes the cell voltage by about 61.5 mV; 0.1 pH unit changes it by about 6.15 mV.

pCO₂ is the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood, in mmHg. The Severinghaus pCO₂ electrode is a pH electrode behind a CO₂-permeable membrane. A thin film of sodium bicarbonate solution sits between the membrane and the glass. CO₂ diffuses in, forms carbonic acid, and lowers the pH of the film. The pH electrode reads that fall; after calibration the signal is displayed as pCO₂.

pO₂ is the partial pressure of oxygen, also in mmHg. The Clark pO₂ electrode is a polarographic cell. A platinum cathode is held at about −0.65 V against an Ag/AgCl anode, and an oxygen-permeable membrane covers the cell. Oxygen crosses the membrane and is reduced at the cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. The current is proportional to pO₂.

Bicarbonate is calculated, not measured, from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation. Base excess is the amount of acid needed to bring pH back to 7.40 at pCO₂ 40 mmHg; normal is −2 to +2 mmol/L. Total CO₂ = [HCO₃⁻] + 0.03 × pCO₂, in mmol/L.

blocks.where: 6.1 is the pKa of carbonic acid at 37 °C; [HCO₃⁻] is in mmol/L; pCO₂ is in mmHg; 0.03 is the CO₂ solubility in mmol/(L·mmHg).

sections.h3: Running a sample and reading the pattern

items: Take arterial blood into a heparinised syringe; the radial artery is common.
Remove air bubbles, cap the syringe and label it.
Run the sample within minutes; if delayed, keep it on ice and correct for temperature.
Calibrate with two gas mixtures of known pCO₂ and pO₂ and with pH buffers; run quality control serum.
Read pH, pCO₂ and pO₂; check the calculated HCO₃⁻ and base excess.

blocks.text: Room air has pO₂ about 150 mmHg and pCO₂ about 0 mmHg. An air bubble therefore raises pO₂ and lowers pCO₂. The chamber is held at 37 °C because the electrodes are calibrated at that temperature; a cool sample gives a falsely low pCO₂ and a falsely high pH. Some syllabi call this an ABG (arterial blood gas) analyser.

figure.caption: Arterial sample enters a 37 °C chamber; three electrodes measure pH, pCO₂ and pO₂, and the analyser calculates bicarbonate and base excess. Notice that only the three electrodes measure directly.

spec.title: Blood gas analyser electrodes
spec.aria: The arterial sample enters a chamber at 37 °C where three separate electrodes measure pH, pCO₂ and pO₂, and the computer displays these three and calculates bicarbonate and base excess from them.

examples.question: A blood gas analyser reports pH 7.32, pCO₂ 30 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L at 37 °C. Check the bicarbonate value with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and classify the acid–base state.
steps: pH 7.32 is below 7.35, so there is acidaemia. HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L is below 22 mmol/L, so the cause is metabolic. pCO₂ 30 mmHg is below 35 mmHg, so the lungs are compensating.
examples.answer: pH = 7.32, so the sample shows metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.
examples.check:
import math
hco3 = 15.0
pco2 = 30.0
ratio = hco3 / (0.03 * pco2)
ph = 6.1 + math.log10(ratio)
print(f"{ph:.2f}")

traps: Mixing mmHg and kPa. Normal pCO₂ is 35–45 mmHg, which is about 4.7–6.0 kPa; do not put a kPa number into a formula written for mmHg.
Forgetting the 37 °C condition. A cool sample gives a falsely low pCO₂ and a falsely high pH, because the electrode slope and the blood equilibria change with temperature.
Leaving an air bubble in the syringe. Room air raises pO₂ and lowers pCO₂, so the printout can look like hyperoxia with respiratory alkalosis.
Treating the printed HCO₃⁻ as a measured value. It is calculated from pH and pCO₂, so an error in pCO₂ moves the HCO₃⁻ value.
Reversing the sign of base excess. A positive base excess means metabolic alkalosis; a negative base excess means metabolic acidosis.

quiz.q: Define pH and give the normal arterial pH range.
quiz.a: pH = −log₁₀ a(H⁺), where a(H⁺) is hydrogen ion activity in mol/L. Normal arterial pH is 7.35–7.45.

quiz.q: Why does a glass pH electrode need an amplifier with very high input impedance?
quiz.a: The glass bulb has very high resistance. If the amplifier draws current, the cell voltage is loaded and falls. A high input impedance means almost no current flows, so the measured voltage stays close to the true electrode potential.

quiz.q: Calculate pH from [HCO₃⁻] = 24 mmol/L and pCO₂ = 40 mmHg at 37 °C.
A syringe has a small air bubble and the sample is run late. What happens to pO₂, pCO₂ and pH, and why?
quiz.a: Room air has pO₂ near 150 mmHg and pCO₂ near 0 mmHg. Oxygen enters the sample, so pO₂ rises. Carbon dioxide leaves the sample, so pCO₂ falls. A fall in pCO₂ tends to raise pH. The result can falsely suggest respiratory alkalosis.

quiz.q: Why does the Severinghaus electrode have a bicarbonate layer behind its membrane?
quiz.a: The bicarbonate layer is a thin pH-sensitive solution. CO₂ crosses the membrane, forms carbonic acid and changes the pH of this layer. The glass pH electrode then reads that pH change, which is calibrated as pCO₂.

quiz.q: At 37 °C the pH electrode slope is 61.5 mV per pH unit. pH falls from 7.40 to 7.20. Find the change in cell voltage.
quiz.a: ΔpH = 7.40 − 7.20 = 0.20. Voltage change = 61.5 × 0.20 = 12.3 mV. With E = E⁰ − 61.5 × pH, the cell voltage rises by about 12.3 mV.

quiz.q: A result shows pH 7.50, pCO₂ 30 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 23 mmol/L. Classify the acid–base state.
quiz.a: pH 7.50 is above 7.45, so there is alkalaemia. pCO₂ 30 mmHg is below 35 mmHg, so the primary change is respiratory. HCO₃⁻ 23 mmol/L is within 22–26 mmol/L. This is respiratory alkalosis.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern blood gas analysers often add co-oximetry to measure haemoglobin species, electrolytes and lactate on the same cartridge. Point-of-care analysers now sit in clinics, not only in laboratories. Research moves toward optical and ISFET sensors that need less blood. Search for “Severinghaus electrode”, “Clark electrode”, “base excess” and “point-of-care blood gas”.
